title: feat(signers): secp256r1 signature verification primitives
description: Add secp256r1 (P-256) signing and verification primitives, and the ScVal shape a passkey smart wallet's `__check_auth` decodes.
why: Passkey wallets are the main reason custom account contracts exist in practice. Without P-256 primitives every passkey user hand-rolls a `SignerFunc` and gets the byte layout wrong in their own way.
criteria: P-256 sign and verify over a 32-byte payload, using crypto/ecdsa.
Signature encoded in the low-S normalised form the host expects, with a test proving a high-S signature is rejected or normalised.
An `ScVal` builder for the passkey signature struct, with the map keys in sorted order.
`go test ./...` covers valid, malformed and high-S inputs.
guidance: New `secp256r1.go` at package root, mirroring how `signer.go` builds the ed25519 account shape.
Do not invent the signature layout: cite the wallet contract or SEP it comes from.
Keep verification separate from the Signer implementation so it can be reused by the verification engine.

title: feat(signers): parse WebAuthn assertions
description: Parse a WebAuthn assertion into the parts a Soroban passkey wallet needs: `authenticatorData`, `clientDataJSON`, the signature, and the challenge the browser actually signed.
why: A WebAuthn signature is not over the payload directly — it is over `authenticatorData || SHA-256(clientDataJSON)`. Getting this wrong produces signatures that verify locally and fail on-chain.
criteria: Parser extracts authenticatorData, clientDataJSON and signature from a WebAuthn assertion.
The challenge embedded in clientDataJSON is checked against the expected soroauth payload, and a mismatch is an error.
Malformed JSON, missing fields and a truncated authenticatorData are all rejected with distinct errors.
Table-driven tests including at least one assertion captured from a real authenticator.
guidance: New `webauthn.go`. Keep it dependency-free if possible; base64url decoding is standard library.
The challenge check is the security-critical part — it is what binds the browser ceremony to this entry.
Record in the doc comment which WebAuthn level/spec section the layout comes from.

title: feat(signers): PasskeySigner implementing the Signer interface
description: A `PasskeySigner` that takes a WebAuthn assertion and returns the `ScVal` a passkey wallet expects, wired through the existing `Signer` interface.
why: This is the piece contributors actually call. It joins the P-256 primitives and the assertion parser to the rest of soroauth so passkey accounts work with `AuthorizeEntry`, `AuthorizeAll` and the CLI unchanged.
criteria: `NewPasskeySigner` returns a `Signer` whose `Address()` is the wallet's C… address.
`Sign` verifies the assertion against the payload before returning, the way `NewEd25519Signer` verifies itself.
A mismatch returns `ErrSignatureMismatch`.
Works end to end through `AuthorizeEntry` with `ForAddress`, with a test.
guidance: Follow the `ed25519Keypair` seam pattern in `signer.go` so the verification guard is testable with a lying signer.
The assertion is supplied by the caller (the browser ceremony happens elsewhere); this type must not try to perform WebAuthn itself.
Document that the ScVal shape targets a specific wallet contract, since unlike the classic account signature there is no single host-defined format.

title: test(golden): passkey vectors from a real wallet library
description: Generate golden vectors for the passkey signature shape from an existing passkey wallet library, and assert soroauth reproduces them byte for byte.
why: Hand-written expectations only prove the code agrees with itself. The ed25519 path is trusted because it is checked against @stellar/stellar-sdk; the passkey path needs the same standard before anyone signs with it.
criteria: Vectors generated by a real library, not written by hand, with the library and version pinned.
`golden_test.go` asserts the produced ScVal is byte-identical to the recorded one.
Vectors are committed and regenerate reproducibly, and CI drift-checks them like the existing ones.
The generator refuses to run against a different library version.
guidance: Extend `testdata/gen/` rather than starting a parallel mechanism; see `gen.mjs` for the version-pinning pattern.
If no suitable library exists, say so on the issue before writing vectors by hand — that changes what the vectors prove.
Never edit a vector by hand; see CONTRIBUTING.md.

title: test(e2e): passkey wallet scenario on testnet
description: An e2e scenario that deploys or targets a passkey wallet contract on testnet and submits a transfer authorized by a P-256 signature soroauth produced.
why: Agreement with a reference library and acceptance by a live host are different claims. Scenarios A-E prove the ed25519 and delegate paths on-chain; the passkey path has no such evidence yet.
criteria: A new scenario in `e2e/` behind the existing `e2e` build tag, submitting a real transaction.
The credential arm is decoded back off the submitted envelope and asserted, as the existing scenarios do.
A matching rejection scenario asserts the host's specific error for a bad P-256 signature.
`e2e/RESULTS.md` regenerates with the new scenario included.
guidance: Read `e2e/README.md` first: the two-simulation flow and why rejection scenarios need instruction headroom.
A rejection test that asserts only `status != SUCCESS` will be rejected in review — assert which failure.
Add the scenario id to `requiredScenarios` in `results_test.go` so RESULTS.md cannot silently omit it.

title: feat(cmd): assemble a passkey signature from the CLI
description: Let `soroauth sign` accept a WebAuthn assertion (from a file or stdin) instead of a seed, so passkey flows are scriptable.
why: Passkey signing happens in a browser, then the assertion has to reach a backend. Without CLI support that handoff is bespoke glue in every integration.
criteria: `--assertion <file|->` accepted alongside the existing flags, and mutually exclusive with `--secret-env`.
The resulting entry matches what the library produces for the same assertion.
Malformed assertions fail with a clear message and write nothing to stdout.
guidance: See `cmd/soroauth/sign.go`; results go to stdout and everything else to stderr.
No secret is ever a flag value — an assertion is not a secret, but keep the existing rule visible in --help.

title: feat(signers): user-presence and timeout handling for passkey signers
description: Handle the WebAuthn flags that say whether the user was present and verified, and give callers a way to require them.
why: A passkey assertion can be produced without user verification. A backend signing a payment should be able to insist on UV, and today has no way to express that.
criteria: Options to require user-presence and/or user-verification, off by default with the default documented.
An assertion failing a required flag is rejected before any signature is returned.
Tests cover each flag combination.
guidance: The flags live in `authenticatorData`; cite the spec section for the bit positions.
Fail closed: if the flags cannot be parsed, reject rather than assume.

title: docs: guide to signing for passkey smart wallets
description: A guide walking through the full passkey flow: browser ceremony, assertion transport, soroauth signing, submission.
why: The passkey path touches three systems and the failure modes are non-obvious. A guide is what stops every integrator rediscovering the challenge-binding problem.
criteria: Walks end to end with runnable snippets.
States explicitly which wallet contract the signature shape targets.
Covers the challenge-binding check and why it matters.
guidance: Link it from README and ARCHITECTURE.md.
Do not claim support for wallets that have not actually been tested against.

title: docs: example program for the passkey signer
description: A small runnable example showing `PasskeySigner` used with `AuthorizeEntry`.
why: Examples are compiled and run by `go test`, so unlike prose they cannot rot.
criteria: An `Example` function that compiles and runs.
Uses deterministic inputs so output is stable.
Appears on pkg.go.dev.
guidance: Follow the Go example conventions; see the issue on doc examples for the house style.

title: docs: doc example for secp256r1 primitives
description: Go doc examples for the P-256 sign and verify helpers.
why: The primitives are the piece most likely to be used standalone by someone writing their own signer.
criteria: An `Example` per exported function.
Deterministic, stable output.
Passes under `go test`.
guidance: Keep examples short enough to read on pkg.go.dev without scrolling.

title: feat(signers): remote signer protocol and reference server
description: Define a wire protocol for signing over HTTP, and ship a reference server implementing it plus a client `Signer`.
why: `SignerFunc` exists so signing can happen elsewhere, but everyone invents their own protocol. The interesting parts — transmitting the preimage so the remote end can inspect what it approves rather than blind-signing a digest, and propagating cancellation — are exactly where people get it wrong.
criteria: A documented request/response schema carrying both the preimage and the payload.
A reference server that decodes and logs what it is approving before signing.
A client `Signer` whose context cancellation aborts the in-flight request.
Integration test running client against server.
guidance: The preimage must be transmitted, not just the hash — that is the point of the `Signer` interface taking both.
State clearly what the reference server deliberately does not do: no authentication, no key storage, not production-ready.

title: feat(signers): AWS KMS signer
description: A `Signer` backed by AWS KMS, so the private key never leaves the HSM.
why: Backends that move real value should not hold raw seeds in process memory. KMS is the most common answer and there is no adapter today.
criteria: Signs via KMS and returns the classic account ScVal shape.
Verifies the returned signature against the payload before handing it back.
Region, key id and credentials are configuration, never hard-coded.
Tests use a KMS fake; no test requires live AWS credentials.
guidance: Keep the AWS SDK dependency out of the root module if it would bloat it — a submodule under `signers/awskms` is acceptable and should be discussed on the issue first.
KMS returns DER-encoded signatures; convert carefully and test the conversion.

title: feat(signers): Google Cloud KMS signer
description: A `Signer` backed by Google Cloud KMS.
why: Same reasoning as the AWS adapter, for teams on GCP. Parity between the two keeps soroauth cloud-neutral.
criteria: Signs via Cloud KMS and returns the correct ScVal shape.
Self-verifies before returning.
Tests run against a fake, not live GCP.
guidance: Mirror the structure of the AWS signer so the two read alike.
Land the AWS signer first if both are in flight, so the shared shape is settled once.

title: feat(signers): HashiCorp Vault signer
description: A `Signer` backed by Vault's transit engine.
why: Vault is the common self-hosted answer for teams that will not use a cloud HSM. It completes the managed-signer set.
criteria: Signs via the transit engine and returns the correct ScVal shape.
Self-verifies before returning.
Token renewal and auth failures surface as clear errors, not panics.
Tests run against a Vault dev server or a fake.
guidance: Document the minimum Vault policy the signer needs — least privilege, not root.

title: feat(signers): Ledger hardware wallet signer
description: A `Signer` that signs through a Ledger device.
why: Hardware wallets are what individuals use for meaningful value. A device that cannot display what it signs is a real limitation, and this issue should establish exactly what it can show.
criteria: Signs a soroauth payload through a connected device.
Documents precisely what the device displays for a Soroban auth entry, and what it cannot.
Device absent, locked, or wrong app produce distinct, actionable errors.
Manual test procedure written down, since CI cannot hold a device.
guidance: If the device cannot display the invocation, say so prominently in the doc comment — users will assume it can.
Blind-signing must be an explicit opt-in, never the default.

title: feat(signers): retry and backoff policy for remote signers
description: A shared retry policy for signers that talk to a network, with jittered backoff and a cap.
why: Every remote signer will otherwise grow its own retry loop, and a naive one can double-sign or hammer a KMS quota.
criteria: Configurable attempts and backoff, off by default.
Retries only on transport errors, never on a signature rejection.
Context cancellation wins over a pending retry.
guidance: A signature rejection is not retryable — retrying it hides a real failure.

title: feat(signers): cancellation and deadline semantics audit
description: Audit every signer for correct context handling and document the guarantees.
why: `Signer.Sign` takes a context, but only the in-tree signers have been checked. A hardware or remote signer that ignores cancellation hangs a caller's request.
criteria: Every in-tree signer honours cancellation, with a test.
The interface doc states what implementers must guarantee.
A signer that cannot be cancelled documents that fact.
guidance: See `TestSignersHonourContextCancellation` for the existing pattern.

title: docs: example remote signer client
description: A runnable example pairing the reference server with a client signer.
why: The protocol issue ships the parts; this shows them working together, which is what integrators copy.
criteria: Runs end to end locally.
Shows the preimage being inspected server-side.
States what is not production-ready.
guidance: Keep it in `examples/`; it should not become a second implementation of the client.

title: docs: choosing a signer
description: A comparison page covering in-memory, multisig, KMS, Vault, Ledger, remote and passkey signers, with the trade-offs.
why: Signer choice is a security decision and the options are not obvious. Today a reader has to infer it from doc comments scattered across files.
criteria: Covers every shipped signer.
States the threat model each addresses.
Says plainly which are unaudited.
guidance: Do not recommend a signer for production use that has no e2e evidence behind it.

title: docs: doc examples for each signer constructor
description: Go doc examples for every exported signer constructor.
why: Constructors are the first thing a reader meets on pkg.go.dev, and examples there cannot rot.
criteria: One `Example` per constructor.
Deterministic output.
Passes under `go test`.
guidance: Match the house style established by the doc-examples issue.

title: docs: example using a KMS signer end to end
description: An example showing a KMS-backed signer authorizing a simulated entry.
why: Cloud KMS setup is fiddly; a worked example removes most of the guesswork.
criteria: Compiles.
Does not require live credentials to build.
Notes the IAM permissions needed.
guidance: Guard any live call behind a build tag so `go test ./...` stays offline.

title: test: Python stellar-sdk parity harness
description: A harness that recomputes every golden vector's preimage and payload with the Python `stellar-sdk` and compares against the recorded values.
why: The vectors prove soroauth agrees with @stellar/stellar-sdk. They do not rule out a bug both share. A third independent implementation is the cheapest way to close that gap.
criteria: Reads `testdata/vectors/*.json` and recomputes preimage and payload.
Any disagreement is reported and investigated, never silently accommodated.
Cases the Python SDK cannot express are skipped loudly, naming which and why.
Runs in CI if coverage is complete enough to be meaningful.
guidance: Do not change a vector to make the harness pass. If Python disagrees, open an issue with the protocol reference.
Pin the Python SDK version the way `gen.mjs` pins the JS one.

title: test: Rust stellar-xdr parity harness
description: The same parity check against the Rust XDR implementation, which is what the host itself uses.
why: Rust is closest to the host. Agreement there is the strongest offline evidence available short of submitting a transaction.
criteria: Recomputes preimage and payload for every vector.
Disagreements reported, not accommodated.
Pinned crate version, reproducible run.
guidance: The e2e contract workspace already pins a Rust toolchain; reuse that setup rather than adding a second.

title: test: differential fuzzing across implementations
description: Fuzz random entries through Go, JS and Python, and fail when the three disagree on the payload.
why: Fixed vectors only cover the cases someone thought of. Differential fuzzing finds the ones nobody did, which is where signature bugs actually live.
criteria: Generates structurally valid random entries across all arms and depths.
Compares payloads across implementations and reports any divergence with a reproducer.
Corpus of divergences is committed as regression vectors.
guidance: Depends on the Python and Rust harnesses; land those first.
A divergence is a release blocker, not a test flake.

title: ci: matrix running every parity suite
description: A CI job matrix that runs the JS drift check plus the Python, Rust and differential suites on a schedule and before releases.
why: A parity harness nobody runs is documentation. This makes divergence a build failure rather than something discovered by a user.
criteria: All suites run on a schedule and on release tags.
A failure names which implementation disagreed and on which vector.
Runtime kept reasonable enough to not be disabled out of frustration.
guidance: Model it on the existing `golden-drift` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.
Pin every toolchain; an unpinned parity run proves nothing.

title: test: publish a parity report artifact
description: Have the parity suites emit a machine-readable report and attach it to CI runs and releases.
why: The README claims byte-for-byte agreement. A per-release artifact turns that from a claim into something a reader can check.
criteria: Report lists every vector and every implementation's verdict.
Attached to release assets.
Regenerates deterministically.
guidance: Keep the format simple enough to diff between releases.

title: test: version the golden vector schema
description: Add an explicit schema version to the vector JSON and make the loader reject versions it does not understand.
why: `golden_test.go` already uses `DisallowUnknownFields`, but a field being *removed* or reinterpreted would pass silently. Parity harnesses in other languages make that worse.
criteria: Every vector carries a schema version.
Loaders in every language reject unknown versions rather than guessing.
Bumping the version is documented in CONTRIBUTING.md.
guidance: Coordinate with the parity harnesses so all readers move together.

title: docs: what the parity suites prove
description: A short page stating exactly what agreement across implementations does and does not establish.
why: Readers reasonably over-read 'proven byte-for-byte'. It is strong evidence and it is not an audit, and the docs should say so in one place.
criteria: States what each suite covers.
States what none of them rule out.
Linked from README and SECURITY.md.
guidance: Keep the honest framing already used in SECURITY.md.

title: feat(wasm): compile the signing core to WebAssembly
description: A WASM build of the preimage, payload and entry-writing core, callable from JavaScript.
why: Passkey signing happens in the browser. Today the payload must be computed server-side and shipped to the client, which means the browser signs bytes it cannot independently derive.
criteria: `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm` build producing a loadable module.
Exposes preimage construction, payload hashing, and writing a signature onto an entry.
Output is byte-identical to the native build for every golden vector.
Build is reproducible and wired into CI.
guidance: Keep the exported surface small; this is a signing core, not the whole library.
The golden vectors are the acceptance test — run them through the WASM build.

title: feat(wasm): TypeScript wrapper package
description: An ergonomic TypeScript package wrapping the WASM module with real types.
why: Raw `syscall/js` interop is unpleasant and easy to misuse. A typed wrapper is what makes the browser path actually adoptable.
criteria: Typed API covering the exported core.
Works in a bundler and from a plain script tag.
Errors surface as JS exceptions with useful messages, not numeric codes.
Tests run in a headless browser or jsdom.
guidance: Mirror the Go names so the two read alike.
Do not re-implement any signing logic in TypeScript — it must call through.

title: ci: npm publishing pipeline for the wasm package
description: Automate building, versioning and publishing the WASM/TS package to npm on a release tag.
why: A browser package that has to be published by hand will drift from the Go release within one cycle.
criteria: Publishes on a tag, with the version derived from the tag.
Refuses to publish if the golden vectors or parity suites fail.
Provenance/signing configured so consumers can verify the artifact.
guidance: Reuse the release automation issue's workflow if it lands first.
Never publish from a branch that is not the tagged commit.

title: feat(examples): browser demo — passkey to submitted transaction
description: A working browser demo: create a passkey, sign a Soroban auth entry with it, submit through an RPC.
why: This is the end-to-end story the passkey work exists for, and having it runnable is what turns several separate subsystems into a provable claim.
criteria: Runs in a browser against testnet.
Derives the payload client-side via WASM rather than trusting a server.
Shows the submitted transaction hash and links to an explorer.
README explains how to run it locally.
guidance: Depends on the WASM core, the TS wrapper and the passkey signer.
Keep secrets out of the demo entirely — passkeys never expose key material, which is the point.

title: ci: enforce a size budget on the wasm build
description: Measure the WASM artifact size in CI and fail if it exceeds an agreed budget.
why: Go WASM binaries grow quickly and silently. A browser package that reaches several megabytes stops being usable without anyone noticing the day it happened.
criteria: Size measured and reported on every build.
Budget enforced, with the number recorded in the repo.
Report shows the delta against the previous release.
guidance: Agree the budget on the issue before enforcing it.

title: refactor(wasm): review the exported API surface
description: Review what the WASM build exposes and narrow it to what browsers actually need.
why: Every exported symbol is a compatibility commitment and adds size. Better to decide the surface deliberately than to inherit it.
criteria: Documented rationale for each exported symbol.
Anything unnecessary removed before the first npm release.
Breaking changes after release follow semver.
guidance: Do this before the first publish; afterwards it is a breaking change.

title: docs: using soroauth from the browser
description: A page covering installation, loading the WASM module, and the passkey flow.
why: The browser path spans several packages and is the least discoverable part of the project.
criteria: Install and load instructions.
A minimal working snippet.
Links the demo.
guidance: Keep it in step with the TS package's README rather than duplicating it.

title: feat: offline verification engine
description: A verification engine that checks whether an entry's signatures actually verify against the payload the entry itself commits to.
why: There is no way today to check an entry short of submitting it. For classic account signatures the library already has everything needed to decide locally, and a failed submission costs fees.
criteria: Rebuilds the payload from the entry and verifies every classic-account signature against it.
Reports per node: verified, unsigned, or a shape it cannot check.
States plainly that a custom account signature cannot be verified offline, since only the contract defines validity.
Covers all three address arms and nested delegate trees.
guidance: Reuse `credentialNodes` in `authorize.go` for the walk rather than writing a second one.
Fail closed: an unrecognised signature shape is 'cannot check', never 'verified'.

title: feat(cmd): soroauth verify subcommand
description: Expose the verification engine as `soroauth verify --entry <b64> --network … --valid-until <n>`.
why: Verification is most useful at the point an operator is about to submit something, which is usually a shell.
criteria: Prints a per-node verdict and exits non-zero if any node fails.
JSON output mode for scripting.
Says explicitly which nodes it could not check and why.
Tested against the golden vectors' signed entries.
guidance: Follow the existing subcommand shape in `cmd/soroauth/`; results to stdout, everything else to stderr.

title: feat: HTTP verification service
description: A small service that accepts an entry and returns a verification report.
why: Wallets and custody systems want a pre-submission check without embedding Go. A service is the lowest-friction way to offer it.
criteria: Documented endpoint accepting an entry plus network and expiration.
Returns the same verdicts as the CLI.
Stateless, holds no keys, and says so.
Integration tests covering valid, partially signed and malformed entries.
guidance: This service must never accept or hold a secret. Verification needs public data only — keep it that way.
Rate limiting and auth are the operator's concern; document that rather than inventing a scheme.

title: feat: batch verification API
description: Verify many entries in one call, reporting per entry.
why: A transaction can carry several entries, and a caller wants one answer for the set, not N round trips.
criteria: Verifies a slice and returns per-entry verdicts.
A failure in one entry does not abort the rest.
Concurrency is bounded and configurable.
guidance: Mirror `AuthorizeAll`'s shape where it makes sense, but note this one deliberately does not fail the batch.

title: feat: report custom account signature shapes best-effort
description: When verification meets a signature it cannot check, describe its shape rather than reporting nothing.
why: 'Cannot check' is honest but unhelpful. Telling the operator it looks like a passkey signature, or an unknown map, lets them reason about it.
criteria: Recognises the known shapes and names them.
Unknown shapes are described structurally, never guessed at.
Never upgrades a description into a verification verdict.
guidance: The line between describing and verifying is the whole point — keep it explicit in the types.

title: docs: what verification can and cannot establish
description: A short page on the limits of offline verification.
why: A verify command invites the belief that a green result means the transaction will succeed. It does not.
criteria: States what a pass does and does not guarantee.
Covers custom accounts, expiration, and nonce consumption.
Linked from the CLI help.
guidance: Match the honest tone of SECURITY.md.

title: test: continuous fuzzing infrastructure
description: Stand up continuous fuzzing that runs beyond CI's time budget and reports findings.
why: Go's fuzzer finds real bugs given hours, and CI can only spare seconds. Without continuous fuzzing the fuzz targets are little more than unit tests.
criteria: Fuzz targets run continuously against the default branch.
Crashes and timeouts open an issue or alert automatically.
Corpus is persisted between runs and committed for regressions.
Documented so a contributor can reproduce a finding locally.
guidance: OSS-Fuzz is the obvious candidate; a self-hosted runner is acceptable if justified on the issue.
Every crash found becomes a committed regression seed.

title: test: fuzz ValidateDelegateOrder
description: A fuzz target over arbitrary entry bytes asserting `ValidateDelegateOrder` never panics and never accepts a mis-ordered or duplicated array.
why: It walks attacker-supplied structure recursively, and its recursion has no depth limit of its own beyond the XDR decoder's.
criteria: `FuzzValidateDelegateOrder` over arbitrary entries.
Properties: never panics; every accepted entry is strictly ascending at every level.
Seed corpus from the golden vectors plus malformed trees.
Deeply nested input covered.
guidance: See `delegates_test.go` for the existing table tests to seed from.

title: test: fuzz Inspect
description: A fuzz target asserting `Inspect` never panics on arbitrary entry bytes.
why: `Inspect` is the function most likely to be pointed at an untrusted entry — that is what it is for.
criteria: `FuzzInspect` over arbitrary bytes.
Never panics; every decodable entry yields either an `EntryInfo` or an error, never a half-populated struct alongside an error.
Seeds from vectors and from entries with empty union arms.
guidance: Empty union arms are the known sharp edge; make sure the corpus includes them.

title: test: fuzz the xdrcopy round-trip
description: Fuzz `xdrcopy.Copy` and assert the copy is always byte-identical and shares no memory.
why: Every non-mutation guarantee in the library rests on this one function.
criteria: Round-trip is byte-identical for any value that marshals.
A value that fails to marshal returns the zero value with an error, never a partial.
No panics.
guidance: See `internal/xdrcopy/copy_test.go` for the aliasing assertions to generalise.

title: test: property test that signed and stored expiration never disagree
description: A property test over generated entries: for every entry `AuthorizeEntry` returns, rebuilding the preimage reproduces the payload its signature verifies against.
why: This is the most dangerous failure the library could have — an entry that looks complete and fails on-chain. Several tests check it incidentally; none asserts it as a property.
criteria: Property holds across all three address arms.
Delegate trees at several depths covered.
Generated expirations include boundary values.
guidance: Reuse the verification engine if it has landed; otherwise verify inline.

title: test: build a fuzz seed corpus from the golden vectors
description: Generate seed corpora for every fuzz target from the committed vectors.
why: A fuzzer starting from random bytes spends most of its budget rediscovering valid XDR. Real entries as seeds get it to the interesting space immediately.
criteria: Corpus generated from vectors, committed, and regenerated by a script.
Every fuzz target has seeds.
Documented in CONTRIBUTING.md.
guidance: Regenerate rather than hand-curate, so it tracks the vectors.

title: docs: running the fuzzers locally
description: Document how to run each fuzz target and reproduce a finding.
why: A fuzz failure from CI is useless if a contributor cannot reproduce it.
criteria: Commands for each target.
How to use a crash artifact.
Where the corpus lives.
guidance: Put it in CONTRIBUTING.md next to the existing test instructions.

title: feat(contracts): policy account with spending limits
description: A custom account contract enforcing per-period spending limits, and soroauth-side support for authorizing against it.
why: Spending limits are the most requested smart-account policy and exercise a path the current fixture does not: a `__check_auth` that inspects the invocation arguments rather than just the signer set.
criteria: Contract enforces a limit per rolling period, with contract unit tests.
An e2e scenario authorizes a within-limit transfer through soroauth.
A matching rejection scenario asserts the contract's specific over-limit error.
Documented as a fixture, not a product.
guidance: Model it on `e2e/contracts/modular-account`; keep it minimal and say so at the top of `lib.rs`.
Reading invocation args inside `__check_auth` is the interesting part — the existing fixture does not do it.

title: feat(contracts): social recovery account
description: A custom account where a guardian set can rotate the signing key after a timelock.
why: Recovery is the other half of why people use smart accounts, and it exercises delegate trees with a time dimension the current fixtures do not reach.
criteria: Contract supports guardian-initiated recovery with a timelock, with unit tests.
An e2e scenario drives a recovery end to end.
A rejection scenario proves recovery before the timelock is refused, asserting the specific error.
Documented as a fixture.
guidance: Keep the guardian set fixed at construction like the existing fixture — no admin functions.

title: feat(contracts): session keys with time-bound delegates
description: A fixture where delegates are valid only within a window, exercising CAP-71 delegation with expiry inside the contract.
why: Session keys are how dApps avoid prompting on every action. This is the clearest real use of nested, revocable delegates.
criteria: Contract accepts a delegate only within its window, with unit tests.
An e2e scenario signs with an in-window session key.
A rejection scenario proves an expired session key is refused with the specific error.
